title: Build it up, one force at a time
oneLine: Start with one node and one log; six failures arrive one by one, and the learner picks the smallest change that survives each, ending with a replicated log and a spoken account of what forced each part.

s01.title: Build it up, one force at a time
s01.body:
Today's job: start with one node and one log, then let six things go wrong, one at a time. Each time, pick the smallest change that survives it. By the end you have built a replicated log, and you can say what forced each part.

The six, in order: a power cut, speed, a lost machine, a split network, an old leader coming back, a read that must be fresh.

A wrong pick or "Not sure" costs nothing. It places a short reading, and that round waits for it. After you read, you get the same job again with new numbers. If you skip the reading, the build carries on as if that part held, and the round keeps waiting.

f1.pinned: Job: decide what must be on disk before a client hears "done".
f1.title: Force 1: the power cut
f1.body:
You have one node and one log file. A client sends "set balance = 70". The node appends the record to the file (the OS holds it in memory) and replies "done".

Assumed costs, not measurements (an SSD flush ranges from about 100 µs to 10 ms): a memory write about 100 ns; a flush to the SSD about 1 ms.

Power dies one millisecond after "done". On restart the client reads balance = 100.

What is the smallest change so this cannot happen?

options.label: Flush the file in the background once a second
options.feedback: Writes acknowledged in that last second are still lost. This only narrows the window.

options.label: Reply "done" only after the record has been flushed to disk
options.feedback:
Yes. "Done" now means "on disk". You paid for it: about 1 ms instead of 100 ns, ten thousand times slower per write. That cost is Force 2.

Built so far: one node, a log, flushed before "done".

options.label: Keep a second copy of the record in memory, in another process
options.feedback: Both copies sit in memory, and a power cut empties all of it.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence, not failure. A short reading is placed, and this round waits for it.

r1.title: A reading, placed
r1.primer: You were choosing what comes before "done". Lamport writes one sentence that orders a disk write against a message. Find it. Which comes first, and what would a restarted node have forgotten if the order were reversed?
r1.passage: Paraphrase of §2.5: an acceptor has to remember what it promised and what it accepted, even through a crash and restart. It does so by recording this in stable storage, and the sentence says where that write sits relative to sending the reply.

f1b.pinned: Job: decide what must be on disk before a client hears "done".
f1b.title: Force 1 again: a replica's "stored"
f1b.body:
Same job, a different place. The build now has a leader and one replica. The replica receives a record, keeps it in memory, and immediately replies "stored". The leader counts that reply and tells the client "done".

A moment later the replica loses power, before it flushed anything.

Which change keeps "done" honest?

options.label: The replica flushes every 10 ms in the background
options.feedback: A write acknowledged inside those 10 ms is still gone. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: The replica replies "stored" only after its own flush
options.feedback:
Right. The same rule where a reply is a promise: a node's "stored" is worth only what survives its restart.

Built so far: a log, flushed before any reply that counts.

options.label: After the restart, the leader asks the replica to say "stored" again
options.feedback: The first reply was already counted and the client already heard "done". Asking later cannot take that back. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

f2.pinned: Job: raise writes per second while every write still waits for its flush.
f2.title: Force 2: speed
f2.body:
So far: one log, flushed before "done".

Assume one log device that does one flush at a time, 1 ms each. One write per flush means:
1 s ÷ 1 ms = 1,000 writes per second, at most.

Your service needs 10,000 per second.

Which change gets there without bringing the power-cut problem back?

options.label: Run ten threads, each flushing its own write
options.feedback: The device still does one flush at a time, 1 ms each. The ceiling stays 1,000 per second.

options.label: Writes arriving during a flush wait, then share the next flush
options.feedback:
Yes. Writes in flight at once = rate × wait = 10,000 per second × 0.001 s = 10. Each flush carries about 10 writes, every client still waits for its flush, and the ceiling rises tenfold. The cost: a write may wait up to one flush for company.

Built so far: a log, flushed before "done", in groups.

options.label: Reply "done" first and flush in the background
options.feedback: Faster, and the power cut from Force 1 is back: "done" no longer means "on disk".

options.label: Buy a CPU twice as fast
options.feedback: The wait is the 1 ms flush, not the 100 ns of CPU work. Twice as fast changes almost nothing.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence, not failure. A short reading is placed, and this round waits for it.

r2.title: A reading, placed
r2.primer: One sentence in this paper buys more throughput from the same protocol. Find it, and ask which fixed cost it spreads across many commands. (The 1984 origin, DeWitt et al. §5.2, is link-only.)
r2.passage: Paraphrase of §4.2: the authors batch several submitted values into one proposal, so one run of the protocol carries many of them.

f2b.pinned: Job: raise writes per second while every write still waits for its flush.
f2b.title: Force 2 again: new numbers
f2b.body:
One log device, one flush at a time, now 2 ms each.

One write per flush:
1 s ÷ 2 ms = 500 writes per second, at most.

The service needs 4,000 per second, and every write still waits for its flush.

On average, how many writes must each flush carry?

options.feedback: 2 × 500 = 1,000 per second. Short of 4,000. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.
4 × 500 = 2,000 per second. Still short. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

Right: 4,000 per second × 0.002 s = 8. The same product is how many writes are waiting at any moment.

Built so far: a log, flushed in groups sized by rate × flush time.
That is the ceiling you started from, per second, not a batch size. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

f3.pinned: Job: decide when the leader may say "done" now that a second machine exists.
f3.title: Force 3: a lost machine
f3.body:
So far: a log, flushed before "done", in groups.

The leader's machine can burn, and its disk goes with it. So you added a replica. A round trip between them is about 0.5 ms in one datacenter.

Today the leader says "done" after its own flush, and sends the record to the replica in the background. The leader's machine burns. The replica takes over. A write the client was told was done is gone.

What is the smallest change so an acknowledged write survives a dead machine?

options.label: Send records to the replica faster, in smaller pieces
options.feedback: Faster shrinks the gap between "done" and "copied"; it does not close it.

options.label: Say "done" only after the replica has also flushed the record
options.feedback:
"Done" now means "on two disks". It costs one more round trip, about 0.5 ms, per group of writes.

New problem: with two machines, if the replica is down the leader cannot say "done" at all. That is Force 4.

Built so far: a log, flushed on two machines before "done".

options.label: Flush the leader's disk twice
options.feedback: Both flushes are on the machine that burned.

options.label: Copy the leader's disk every night
options.feedback: A copy restores yesterday. Everything acknowledged since is not in it.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence, not failure. A short reading is placed, and this round waits for it.

r3.title: A reading, placed
r3.primer: A majority makes the failover decision, yet acknowledged writes vanish. As you read, ask: what did the majority agree on, and what did the primary's "OK" certify?
r3.passage: Setup, summarised (not a quote): a Redis primary with replicas is partitioned; a majority of monitor processes promote a new primary; writes the old primary had acknowledged are missing afterwards.

f3b.pinned: Job: decide when the leader may say "done" now that a second machine exists.
f3b.title: Force 3 again: a vote that lost writes
f3b.body:
A team runs a primary with one backup that copies in the background. Three monitor processes watch them. Two of the three agree the primary is down and promote the backup.

The last 40 writes the old primary acknowledged were never copied. They are gone. Someone says: "We had a majority vote, so this was consensus."

Which statement is right?

options.label: The vote picked who is primary. Nobody checked that the new primary held what the old one had acknowledged.
options.feedback:
Right. A majority chose a leader; it never agreed on the log. Replication is not consensus.

Built so far: acknowledged means held by another machine.

options.label: Three monitors is too few; five would have kept the writes
options.feedback: More voters on who is primary change nothing about what the backup holds. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: The backup flushed too slowly
options.feedback: The writes never reached it before "done". Its flush speed does not enter. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

f4.pinned: Job: choose how many machines must store a write before "done".
f4.title: Force 4: a split network
f4.body:
So far: a leader and two replicas, "done" means held by another machine.

The network splits. Side X: the leader alone. Side Y: both replicas. Clients can reach both sides. Side Y elects a new leader and carries on.

Waiting for all three stalls writes whenever any machine is down. Waiting for one lets the old leader keep saying "done" alone.

How many machines must store a write before "done"?

options.label: One: the leader alone is enough
options.feedback: The isolated leader says "done" on its own disk while side Y accepts different writes. Two histories.

options.label: Three: every machine
options.feedback: One machine down, even rebooting, stops all writes.

options.label: Two: any majority of the three
options.feedback:
Any two groups of two among three machines share a machine. So two different answers can never both be "done", and the shared machine can tell a new leader what was committed. The cost: one slow or dead machine is ignored, but two down stops writes.

Built so far: a log on a majority before "done".

options.label: Whichever side has more clients
options.feedback: Clients can't prove which side is bigger. Both sides can claim it.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence, not failure. A short reading is placed, and this round waits for it.

r4.title: A reading, placed
r4.primer: Lamport picks a size for "large enough" and gives a one-line reason. Find it. What would break if two such sets could be disjoint?
r4.passage: Paraphrase of §2.2: to make sure only one value is chosen, a value counts as chosen when a majority of acceptors have accepted it, and the argument leans on a fact about any two majorities.

f4b.pinned: Job: choose how many machines must store a write before "done".
f4b.title: Force 4 again: five machines
f4b.body:
Five machines. The network splits them into a group of two and a group of three. A teammate says: "Two acks is enough for done."

Pick the smallest number of acks that stops both groups from saying "done" to different writes, while still working with two machines down.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: The group of two and the group of three can each reach two acks, with different writes. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Three
options.feedback:
Right. Any two groups of three among five share a machine, and three still works with two machines down.

Built so far: a log on a majority before "done".

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Safe against disagreeing, but writes stop after the second failure. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

f5.pinned: Job: decide how a machine tells a dead leader's orders from the current leader's.
f5.title: Force 5: the old leader comes back
f5.body:
So far: a leader and two replicas, "done" on a majority.

During the split, side Y elected leader B and committed new writes. Now the network heals. Old leader A never knew. It sends replica 2: "append x = 1". Replica 2 follows B.

A needs two acks, and replica 2 would make two. Each leader's timers are sometimes wrong about the other.

What stops replica 2 from obeying A?

options.label: Replica 2 waits for A's heartbeat timeout before trusting B
options.feedback: A late A and a dead A look the same in an asynchronous network. Safety cannot rest on a timer.

options.label: Every leadership period has a number; messages carry it; a machine rejects any lower number than it has seen
options.feedback:
A term. B's is 4, A's is 3. Replica 2 rejects A and tells it 4, and A steps down. The cost: a number in every message, kept on disk across restarts, so another flush. Timers only decide when to start an election. The numbers keep it safe.

Built so far: a majority log with numbered leaders.

options.label: Replica 2 obeys whichever leader it heard from most recently
options.feedback: Messages arrive late. The most recent arrival can be the oldest leader, which is A here.

options.label: Replica 2 asks the clients which leader to trust
options.feedback: Clients saw both leaders answer. They have no basis either.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence, not failure. A short reading is placed, and this round waits for it.

r5.title: A reading, placed
r5.primer: Raft lists every place a term is compared. List them as you read. What does a server do on a bigger term, and what on a smaller one?

source.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (extended)
source.author: Ongaro, Ousterhout

r5.passage: Short quote: "If a server receives a request with a stale term number, it rejects the request."

f5b.pinned: Job: decide how a machine tells a dead leader's orders from the current leader's.
f5b.title: Force 5 again: a stale message
f5b.body:
Replica C is at term 7. A message arrives: "append entry", term 5.

What does C do?

options.label: Accept it: a leader that has been up longer must know more
options.feedback: Longer up proves nothing. Term 5 is the older leadership. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Reject it silently
options.feedback: C is safe, but the sender never learns it is stale and keeps believing it leads. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Reject it and reply with 7
options.feedback:
Right. The sender sees a bigger term and steps down.

Built so far: a majority log with numbered leaders.

options.label: Accept it and lower its own term to 5
options.feedback: Terms only go up. Going back could let C vote again in a term it already voted in. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

f6.pinned: Job: decide how a leader answers a read without serving old data.
f6.title: Force 6: a read that must be fresh
f6.body:
So far: a majority log with numbered leaders.

Leader B holds the state in memory: a local read costs about 100 ns. Asking a majority "am I still leader?" costs a round trip, about 0.5 ms, five thousand times more.

Suppose B was cut off and replaced, and does not know yet. If it answers from its own copy, a client gets an old value after seeing a newer one from the new leader.

What should B do before answering a read?

options.label: Answer from its own copy; reads change nothing, so they can't break agreement
options.feedback: Reads change nothing, but a deposed leader's copy is old. The client sees time go backwards.

options.label: Answer from any replica, to spread the load
options.feedback: A replica can lag behind what is committed, so it can return old values even when the leader is fine.

options.label: Shorten the leader timeout so a deposed leader notices sooner
options.feedback: Sooner is not sure. Between its last check and the next, it still answers.

options.label: Confirm with a majority that it is still leader, then answer
options.feedback:
Reads write nothing to the log, but they still need agreement about who leads. One round trip with a majority can serve every read that is waiting. A lease can skip that trip if you trust clocks; then the cost moves to clock assumptions.

Built: a replicated log with durable commits, a majority, numbered leaders, and agreed reads.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence, not failure. A short reading is placed, and this round waits for it.

r6.title: A reading, placed
r6.primer: Why can't a master answer reads from its own copy? Find the reason the authors give. Then find which side's lease timeout is shorter, and what that protects against.
r6.passage: Paraphrase of §5.2–5.3: in their system a master serves reads from its own copy only under a lease the other replicas have agreed not to break, and an epoch number kept in the database lets the master abort a request if its own mastership was lost or re-acquired while handling it.

f6b.pinned: Job: decide how a leader answers a read without serving old data.
f6b.title: Force 6 again: fifty thousand reads
f6b.body:
Confirming leadership with a majority takes 0.5 ms, and the leader runs one confirmation at a time. One confirmation per read means:
1 s ÷ 0.5 ms = 2,000 reads per second, at most.

The service gets 50,000 reads per second, and none may be stale.

How should the leader confirm?

options.label: Confirm one read in every 25 and answer the rest locally
options.feedback: The unconfirmed ones may be stale. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: One confirmation covers every read that arrived while it was in flight
options.feedback:
Right. 50,000 per second × 0.0005 s = 25 reads wait at any moment, so one round serves about 25.

Built: a replicated log with agreed reads.

options.label: Add machines so more confirmations run at once
options.feedback: More machines make the majority bigger; the leader still runs one confirmation at a time. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as evidence. This stays parked until next session; the reading is already marked read.

rec.pinned: Job: say the build in your own voice, with what forced each part.
rec.title: Say it out loud
rec.prompt: An interviewer asks: "Why isn't one flushed log enough for your system?" In about a minute, walk from one node to a replicated log. For each part, say what forced it and what it costs. No notes.
rubric: Flush before "done", forced by a power cut; costs about a millisecond per write.
Group commit, forced by the flush ceiling; batch size is rate × flush time.
"Done" only after another machine has flushed it, forced by a lost machine and its disk.
A majority, forced by a split; any two majorities share a machine.
Numbered leaders, forced by timers that cannot tell a late leader from a dead one.
Reads confirm leadership with a majority, because a deposed leader doesn't know it yet.

rw.title: A reading, placed
rw.primer: Your take left several forces unnamed. This paper builds the same log in industry. Count the forced flushes on the critical path, then see what it says about a stable master. Your recording is kept; you can re-take it after reading.
rw.passage: Summary, not a quote: §4.2 describes a master that stays the same across instances and where replicas write to disk before replying; §5.1 covers what happens to the argument when a replica loses what it flushed.

end.title: Where you are
end.body:
You built a log that is flushed before "done", flushed in groups, held by a majority, led by numbered leaders, and read through agreement.

Your ledger holds, in words: the forces you answered on your own; the ones where you chose wrongly or said "Not sure", each with its placed reading; and which of those you read, saved or skipped. Parked rounds come back after their reading.

Your recording is kept with its prompt, the six ideas and the ones you ticked. The weekly review reads it.

Next force: one request fans out to many machines, and the slowest one sets the time.
